title: Whose inflation is it?
hook: Three prices rose by different amounts. How much did this household's costs rise?

doesNotKnow: that a headline rate is a weighted average
that a household's own rate depends on its own mix of spending

misconception: Inflation is the average of how much each price rose.
objective: The learner can explain that an index weights each price rise by its share of spending, so a household that spends half its budget on the item that rose most sees 3.6%, not the plain average 2.7%.

claims.text: A household spending 50% on rent (up 6%), 30% on food (up 2%) and 20% on fun (up 0%) sees its total cost of living rise by 3.6%.
The plain average of the three rises 6, 2 and 0 is 2.7% (2.67).
Rent adds 3.0 percentage points to the overall rise, food 0.6 and fun 0.0 (share x rise).
A price index weights each price by its share of spending, so a household's own inflation depends on its own mix.
claims.source: Definition of a fixed-basket (Laspeyres-type) price index, e.g. standard macroeconomics texts on the consumer price index; the weighted average is the calculation on the stage.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: the shares and rises are invented, the basket is fixed, and households do not switch goods.
claims.source: Assumptions of Demo.tsx; stage chip 'Model: fixed basket, invented numbers'.

recall.question: Rent is 60% of a budget and rises 5%; everything else (40%) is flat. How much did total costs rise?
recall.why: Weight each rise by its share of spending: 0.6 x 5 + 0.4 x 0 = 3%.
